summary:
Earth System Trend Detective is a web app that answers one question for any place on Earth: is it changing here, and is the change real? Users pick a topic (heat, water, land or air), choose a place from a list or click anywhere on an interactive globe, and select a variable such as air temperature, rainfall or soil moisture. The app pulls 45 years (1981–2025) of monthly NASA MERRA-2 data through the NASA POWER API, removes the seasonal cycle variations, fits a long-term trend and tests its significance with two independent tests, a t-test and Mann-Kendall. It then explains the result in plain terms: how fast it is changing, how certain we are, and the odds it is just a fluke.

This makes understanding of Earth-system variable easy without a statistics background. Climate change is usually reported as global averages, but decisions are local. Students, farmers, planners and residents can check what is actually changing where they live, and tell a real trend from natural noise.
details:
Project Name
Trendy Earth

High-Level Project Summary
Trendy Earth is a web app that answers one question for any place on Earth: is it changing here, and is the change real? Users pick a topic (heat, water, land or air), choose a place from a list or click anywhere on an interactive globe, and select a variable such as air temperature, rainfall or soil moisture. The app pulls 45 years (1981–2025) of monthly NASA MERRA-2 data through the NASA POWER API, removes the seasonal cycle, fits a long-term trend and tests its significance with two independent tests, a t-test and Mann-Kendall. It then explains the result in plain language: how fast it is changing, how certain we are, and the odds it is just a fluke.

This makes NASA Earth-system data usable without a statistics background. Climate change is usually reported as global averages, but decisions are local. Students, farmers, planners and residents can check what is actually changing where they live, and tell a real trend from natural noise.

Link to Project Demo
https://github.com/ShwetasreeChowdhury16/nasaspaceapps2026/blob/main/Trendy%20Earth%20%E2%80%93%20NASA%20Space%20Apps%202026%20demo.pdf

Link to Final Project
https://trendyearth.streamlit.app/

Detailed Project Description

What it does
Trendy Earth answers one question for any place on Earth: is this part of the climate changing here, and is the change real? It is built for non-specialists, so every result comes with a plain-language verdict, while the underlying statistics remain visible for experts.

How a user investigates

  1. Choose what to investigate: Heat, Water, Land or Air. The page colour and a subtle animated background (sun, waves, hills, wind) follow the topic.
  2. Choose where: 12 preset places spanning cities, deserts, rainforest, semi-arid, polar, mountain and temperate regions, or click any point on the interactive globe to investigate it live.
  3. Choose the clue: each topic offers variables phrased as everyday questions (“Is it getting hotter?”, “Is the soil drying out?”) with plain definitions.
  4. Read the verdict: a headline such as “Yes, air temperature here is rising: about X °C every 10 years”, a confidence level, and four cards: How fast is it changing? How sure are we about that speed? Could it just be a fluke? Does a second check agree? Each card carries an evidence rating, and an expandable guide explains what each measure means and what counts as strong evidence.

Further tabs let users test every variable at a place and rank what is changing most (with suggestions based on the region type), see the raw data and the seasonal cycle that is removed, compare the same variable across contrasting climates, view a regional map of trends per 0.5° grid cell marked by significance, and read the full method and its limits. Every series can be downloaded as CSV.

How it works

  • Data: monthly NASA POWER data (MERRA-2 reanalysis), 1981-2025, ~0.5° grid, 9 variables: T2M, T2M_MAX, TS, PRECTOTCORR, RH2M, GWETROOT, ALLSKY_SRF_ALB, PS, WS2M.
  • Deseasonalising: each calendar month’s long-term mean is subtracted to leave the anomaly (difference from normal); complete years are averaged.
  • Trend: ordinary least-squares regression gives the slope per decade, its 95% confidence interval and a t-test p-value.
  • Second check: the non-parametric Mann-Kendall test and Sen’s slope, which do not assume a straight line or normal errors and are robust to single extreme years. Our implementation was validated against the pymannkendall package.
  • Verdict: both tests are combined into a confidence level and translated into plain language, including the chance (“about 1 in N”) that random variation alone would produce such a trend.

Benefits

  • Local and personal: any point on Earth, not just global averages.
  • Honest: it says “no clear trend” when the data do not support one, and explains why.
  • Accessible: no account, no API key, no statistics background needed.
  • Consistent: a single NASA source means every variable shares the same grid, period and processing, so comparisons are fair.

What we hope to achieve
To make NASA’s long-term Earth data a tool people use to answer their own questions, in classrooms, community planning, agriculture and journalism, and to build intuition for the difference between a real trend and noise.

Limits and future work
Linear trends only; reanalysis is model-based; a 0.5° cell averages over roughly 50 km; significance shows that something changed, not why. Next steps: more variables (sea surface temperature, sea ice, snow cover, vegetation), seasonal trends, change-point detection and projections for confirmed trends with uncertainty.

Tools and languages
Python, Streamlit, D3.js (interactive globe), Plotly (charts and maps), pandas, NumPy, SciPy, requests; deployed on Streamlit Community Cloud; code on GitHub.

Use of AI
I chose the challenge and directed the design: globe-based place selection, the guided topic → place → variable flow, plain-language verdicts for non-experts, and topic-themed visuals. Claude (Anthropic), a large language model, was used as a coding and writing assistant. It helped debug the code, implement the statistical tests (checked against the pymannkendall package), build the styling and animated backgrounds, and draft the documentation, which I reviewed. No AI-generated images, video or audio are used. All data and results come from NASA POWER and the analysis code. This is also stated in the README of the GitHub repository.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI) (judges don’t see this field)
Yes. I chose the challenge and directed the design: globe-based place selection, the guided topic → place → variable flow, plain-language verdicts for non-experts, and topic-themed visuals. I used Claude (Anthropic), a large language model, as a coding and writing assistant. It helped debug the Python/Streamlit code, implement and check the statistical tests (validated against the pymannkendall package), build the page styling, animated SVG backgrounds and the D3 globe, and draft the documentation and this submission text, which I reviewed and edited. No SI-generated images, video or audio are used, and no NASA branding was generated. SI assistance is acknowledged in the “Use of AI” section of the GitHub README and in the Detailed Project Description.

NASA Data

  • NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources) API, NASA Langley Research Center – https://power.larc.nasa.gov – monthly point and regional data, 1981-2025, accessed through the temporal/monthly endpoint.
  • MERRA-2 (Modern-Era Retrospective analysis for Research and Applications, Version 2), NASA Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO) – the reanalysis underlying the POWER meteorology variables.
  • Variables used: T2M (air temperature at 2 m), T2M_MAX (daily maximum temperature), TS (earth skin temperature), PRECTOTCORR (bias-corrected precipitation), RH2M (relative humidity at 2 m), GWETROOT (root-zone soil wetness), ALLSKY_SRF_ALB (all-sky surface albedo), PS (surface pressure), WS2M (wind speed at 2 m).
  • Challenge resources: “Be an Earth System Trend Detective!” challenge page and its listed resources.

NASA data is the core of the project: every chart, test and verdict is computed directly from it.

Space Agency Partner Data and Other References
Data

  • NASA POWER Project, NASA Langley Research Center: https://power.larc.nasa.gov
  • Gelaro, R. et al. (2017), The Modern-Era Retrospective Analysis for Research and Applications, Version 2 (MERRA-2), Journal of Climate, 30, 5419-5454.

Methods

  • Mann, H. B. (1945), Nonparametric tests against trend, Econometrica, 13, 245-259.
  • Kendall, M. G. (1975), Rank Correlation Methods, Griffin, London.
  • Sen, P. K. (1968), Estimates of the regression coefficient based on Kendall’s tau, JASA, 63, 1379-1389.

Open-source software

  • Streamlit (Apache 2.0), Plotly (MIT), pandas (BSD-3), NumPy (BSD-3), SciPy (BSD-3), requests (Apache 2.0), pymannkendall (MIT; used only to validate our implementation).
  • D3.js (ISC) and topojson-client (ISC) for the interactive globe.
  • world-atlas map data (ISC), derived from Natural Earth (public domain), for the globe; Natural Earth data via Plotly for the regional map.

AI assistance

  • Claude (Anthropic), used as a coding and writing assistant as described above.

No Space Agency Partner data was used. No copyrighted images, music or text were used.
